questions.q: What password does `sudo` prompt for when a permitted user runs a privileged command?
options: The root account's password
The calling user's own password
No password is ever required
The password of whichever user is listed first in /etc/passwd
questions.explain: sudo authenticates the person running the command with their own password, as long as sudoers grants them permission — unlike su, which requires the target account's password.

questions.q: Why should /etc/sudoers always be edited with visudo instead of a regular text editor?
options: visudo adds color syntax highlighting
visudo is faster to open
visudo validates the file's syntax before saving, preventing an edit that could lock out every admin
visudo automatically backs the file up to the cloud
questions.explain: A broken sudoers file can block every sudo command on the system. visudo checks syntax before committing the change, so an error is caught instead of saved.

questions.q: In a sudoers rule, what does a `%` prefix before a name mean, as in `%ops ALL=(ALL) ALL`?
options: The rule applies to a percentage of login attempts
The rule applies to a group, not an individual user
The rule is commented out and has no effect
The rule only applies on weekends
questions.explain: A leading % marks the name as a group rather than a single user, so every member of that group gets the granted access.

questions.q: What is the main risk of writing `someuser ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL` for a real human account?
options: It makes the account unable to log in at all
It removes the password prompt for every command, undermining the accountability sudo is meant to provide
It disables sudo logging entirely across the whole server
It is functionally identical to deleting the account
questions.explain: NOPASSWD: ALL on a human account lets anyone with that session run any command as root with no password check, erasing the friction and much of the audit value sudo normally provides. NOPASSWD should be scoped to specific, narrow commands.

questions.q: Which command tells you exactly which sudo commands the current user is permitted to run?
options: sudo -l
sudo -k
whoami
visudo -c
questions.explain: sudo -l lists the commands the current user is allowed to run under sudo, based on the active sudoers rules.
